definition: Openly hostile and eager to argue or pick a fight.
example: After losing the debate, he grew belligerent and challenged every point the judges had made.
nuance: Belligerent describes hostile behavior shown in the moment, while bellicose suggests a lasting temperament inclined toward fighting.
prompt: A referee calls a foul against the home team during a youth basketball game.
options: The belligerent coach shouted at the referee and refused to return to the bench.
The belligerent coach thanked the referee warmly and shook hands after the whistle.
The belligerent coach reviewed game film every night to help her players improve.
The belligerent coach cheered so loudly for both teams that the whole gym smiled.
reasons: Yelling and defying the official is the kind of open hostility the word describes.
Warm thanks and a handshake are friendly, the reverse of a combative attitude.
Steady hard work suggests diligent, a sound-alike, not someone itching for a fight.
Being loud is not the same as being hostile; cheerful noise has no aggression in it.

practice.prompt: A neighbor is upset about a tree branch hanging over the fence.
options: The belligerent neighbor stormed over and demanded, in a raised voice, that we cut it today.
The belligerent neighbor politely asked if we might trim the branch sometime this spring.
The belligerent neighbor, worn out after a week of storms, sighed at yet another fallen limb.
The belligerent neighbor measured the branch with a tape and wrote its length in a notebook.
reasons: Storming over and making angry demands shows an aggressive, confrontational manner.
A polite, patient request is courteous, the opposite of picking a fight.
Weariness from repeated trouble fits beleaguered, a look-alike, not hostility.
Calmly taking a measurement shows no anger or urge to argue at all.
